questions.title: Cheese available per American
questions.hint: Pizza chains, fast food, processed cheese and a shift from drinking milk to eating it all pushed on American appetites.
questions.explanation: It rose to 38.1 lb in 2020, from 7.7 lb in 1950. Pizza, cheeseburgers and packaged shredded cheese drove it up almost every year. Availability is supply per person (production plus imports, minus exports and stock changes), not measured eating.

questions.title: Death rate from cancer in the United States
questions.hint: Smoking causes many cancers, and lung cancer deaths follow smoking rates with a lag of decades.
questions.explanation: It fell to 159 in 2015, from 187 in 1945. Age-adjusted to the 2000 US population. How causes are coded changed with each revision of the international classification (1949, 1958, 1968, 1979, 1999), which moves some deaths between causes.

source.attribution: US CDC, National Center for Health Statistics

questions.title: Share of business locations in the United States that opened that year
questions.unitLabel: % of employer business locations that were new that year
questions.hint: This counts only businesses with employees, and each shop, office or plant separately.
questions.explanation: It fell to 10.6% in 2023, from 15.1% in 1978. From the Census Bureau’s Business Dynamics Statistics, built from its register of every employer business.

questions.title: Crude oil production in the United States
questions.hint: Old oil fields decline unless new ones are found or new drilling methods unlock more oil.
questions.explanation: It rose to 13.7 in 2025, from 6.8 in 1955.

questions.title: Executions carried out in the United States
questions.hint: The Great Depression’s crime wave, a slow loss of appetite for the electric chair, a Supreme Court ruling, a comeback in the tough-on-crime 1990s, DNA exonerations, and drug makers refusing to supply lethal-injection drugs.
questions.explanation: It went from 21 in 1963 to a high of 68 in 1998, then ended at 24 in 2023. Executions stopped entirely from 1968, and in 1972 the Supreme Court (Furman v. Georgia) struck down existing death penalty laws. After it allowed new ones in 1976 they resumed and climbed to 98 in 1999, then fell as death sentences dried up and lethal-injection drugs became hard to get. Civil executions only.
